speaker: Susan Collins
occasion: Speech 'The U.S. Economy: Resilience Amid Risks and Uncertainty', Boston Economic Club (official PDF text)
quote: I could envision a scenario in which some policy tightening is needed to ensure that inflation returns durably to 2 percent in a timely manner
summary: Collins says it will likely be important to keep the slightly restrictive stance for some time and that more than five years of above-target inflation has reduced her patience for looking through another supply shock. She hopes normalization can resume later this year, but can envision a scenario requiring some tightening, although that is not her most likely outlook. Policy is well positioned for now.
old_note: Opens the door to a hike and says patience for looking through supply shocks is reduced; hike is a risk scenario, not her baseline.

speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
occasion: Speech "Leveraging Modern Payments Infrastructure in Community Banking", Future of Banking Conference, Kansas City, Mo.
quote: However, I see continued inflation as the most pressing risk to the economy.
summary: Mostly a payments and FedNow speech. In a short outlook passage Schmid said the economy is resilient and the labor market is functioning, but inflation is still too high and is the most pressing risk.
old_note: Only a brief outlook passage; inflation named as the dominant risk, no rate-path statement.

speaker: Seth Carpenter
occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast, mid-year global economic outlook (recorded Thursday May 14, 10am New York)
quote: We expect the Fed to now stay on hold all the way through 2026
summary: Carpenter said central banks have become less accommodative as inflation risks rose; Morgan Stanley expects the Fed on hold through 2026 and, if inflation does come down, two cuts in the first half of 2027.
old_note: Hold through 2026; next move still a cut in 2027.

speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (May 16 edition, after the Senate confirmed Warsh)
quote: He takes over a central bank that has allowed inflation to run above its 2% target for over five years
summary: El-Erian says Warsh inherits one of the hardest starts of any incoming chair: a new surge in inflation, risks to growth, a Fed with key policy errors behind it, political attack and an urgent need for operational reform. He expects Fed minutes and speeches to be parsed for recognition of growing policy dilemmas and escalating risks to financial stability.
old_note: Stresses a two-sided dilemma (inflation surge versus growth and financial-stability risks); criticism of past inflation overshoot is backward-looking.

speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
occasion: Fox News Sunday Morning Futures interview
quote: It’s just not possible, in my view, to cut interest rates when the two-year Treasury is almost 50 basis points higher than the Fed funds rate.
summary: Gundlach said the Fed cannot cut with the two-year yield almost 50bp above fed funds and that DoubleLine's models point to the next headline CPI starting with a four. He said stocks rally when the Fed does nothing about inflation, and that private credit always seems to need new investors.
old_note: Rules out cuts and says the Fed is not addressing inflation; no explicit hike call in the quoted text, so +1.

speaker: Aditya Bhave
occasion: Reuters poll of economists (May 14-19)
quote: It feels like if they are going to have their next move as a cut, it's more likely to be next year than this year,
summary: Bhave said both hikes and cuts are feasible, the base case is a hold and it is a close call between the other two; if the next move is a cut it is more likely in 2027 than 2026.
old_note: Base case hold with two-sided risk; explicitly says hikes are feasible but not the base case.

speaker: Jamie Dimon
occasion: Bloomberg Television interview at JPMorgan's China summit, Shanghai (aired May 21 Shanghai time, late May 20 US Eastern)
quote: They could be much higher than they are today,
summary: Dimon told Bloomberg Television that interest rates could be much higher than today and that the world may have moved from a saving glut to not enough savings. The remark came as long Treasury yields hit multi-year highs and markets priced Fed hikes.
old_note: Forecast that rates can go much higher (savings shortage, deficits, inflation). It is about the level of rates broadly, not an explicit call for Fed hikes, so +1 rather than +2. Date: the interview video was posted about 23:18 ET on May 20; articles are dated May 21.

occasion: Research note dated May 21, reported by Invezz May 22
quote: But recent data and Fedspeak make us sceptical that he will be able to convince a majority of the FOMC to go along with rate cuts in 2026.
summary: Nomura dropped its forecast of two cuts later in 2026 and now expects no cuts this year, citing higher inflation readings and waning support among Fed officials for easing; it doubts Warsh can win an FOMC majority for cuts.
old_note: Moves to no cuts in 2026 (hold); no hike call on the page.

speaker: Phillip Lee
occasion: Goldman Sachs The Markets podcast (recorded May 21, 2026), transcript PDF
quote: the Fed will stay on hold for a bit
summary: Lee (a sales-desk view, not GS Research) said the base case has moved from when and how much the Fed cuts to how long it stays on hold; he finds the roughly 30bp of hikes priced into 2027 a bit tough, though inflation keeps the Fed on hold at best.
old_note: Base case is a hold of uncertain length; notes hikes are priced but does not forecast them.

speaker: Jamie Dimon
occasion: Bernstein Strategic Decisions Conference, New York
quote: there will be more inflation than people expect
summary: Dimon repeated his view that inflation will be higher than people expect and that asset prices, including JPMorgan's stock, are high. He said clients are gung ho and there is a lot of exuberance. eFinancialCareers reports he said the next crisis will not be systemic but credit losses will be much worse than people think.
old_note: Inflation-higher-than-expected forecast leans tighter; no explicit call on what the Fed should do in the quotes found. His reported comments on Warsh and the Fed balance sheet could not be verified as direct quotes.

speaker: Alberto Musalem
occasion: Keynote "How Should the Promise of Higher Productivity Growth Change the Reality of Monetary Policy Today?" and Q&A (moderator Claire Jones, FT), Reykjavik Economic Conference, Iceland
quote: A better policy would be to lean against demand and inflation pressures today.
summary: Musalem argued it would be risky to rely on future AI-driven productivity gains to solve today's inflation problem. He noted the real policy rate is below the FOMC's long-run neutral, inflation is meaningfully above target and longer-term inflation expectations are creeping higher, and said holding policy rates too low could push long-term rates up. He called for a vigilant policy focused on restoring price stability and said he would adjust only if evidence shows productivity is pulling inflation to target. In the Q&A (Reuters, https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-28/fed-policymakers-eye-rate-hike-scenarios-ai-debate-deepens) he said "If we don't see disinflation in the next one to two quarters, that would concern me" and that risks have tilted more toward inflation than the labor market.
old_note: Inflation risk dominates and he says policy should lean against demand; says the real rate is below neutral. No explicit call for a hike in the prepared text, so +1 not +2.

speaker: Alberto Musalem
occasion: Bloomberg TV interview with Stephanie Flanders at the Reykjavik Economic Conference (auto-generated transcript published with the Bloomberg Talks podcast clip, https://omny.fm/shows/bloomberg-talks/feds-alberto-musalem-talks-fed-policy)
quote: There is a scenario where inflation remains high, there's no disinflation in the next quarter or two, and in that scenario, the economy will probably require a hike.
summary: Musalem said the real policy rate is around 0.5%, below the 1% the Committee sees as neutral, so policy is at or slightly below long-run neutral. He supported the April hold but thought the statement's easing bias was no longer consistent with the outlook and a balance of risks that has shifted toward inflation. Hike, cut or hold depends on the scenario: no disinflation in a quarter or two would probably require a hike; a material weakening in the second half would mean no hikes, maybe a cut. He said the probability of considering a rate increase "has to be greater than zero", and that shrinking the balance sheet is better done by reducing reserve demand than by cutting supply.
old_note: Open to hiking and wanted the easing bias removed, but frames a hike as scenario-dependent rather than needed now; +1 not +2. Transcript is machine-generated (names are garbled in places); the quoted sentence matches the Reuters account of the interview.

speaker: Jamie Dimon
occasion: CNBC interview at the Reagan National Economic Forum
quote: Interest rates are gravity to asset prices
summary: Dimon said the market is exuberant, that there is hype in some of it, and that very low credit spreads are a risk. He named inflation as his most immediate concern and said it can easily hit 4% this year. He said that if something goes wrong asset prices can come down because interest rates are gravity to asset prices.
old_note: Inflation (could hit 4%) is his top risk and he ties higher rates to asset-price risk; leans tighter. No explicit statement on what the Fed should do.

speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
occasion: Speech "The Local and the Global in Monetary Policy", Reykjavik Economic Conference, Iceland (discussion moderated by Stephanie Flanders)
quote: We must continue to signal our commitment to price stability and our willingness to take the actions necessary to achieve our mandate.
summary: Schmid said the oil disruption is adding to inflation (CPI 3.8% in the 12 months to April, 2.8% excluding energy), that with inflation above 2% for over five years it is not the time to let down the guard, and that he places little stock in the latest run-up being transitory. He sees the labor market in balance; inflation is his primary concern in setting policy. In comments after the speech (Reuters, https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-29/feds-schmid-warns-against-viewing-oil-shock-transitory) he said "We're not very restrictive at this stage" and that officials need to start considering what tools they have to make policy a little more restrictive, including looking at the balance sheet again.
old_note: Inflation dominates; in Q&A he said policy is not very restrictive and tools to add restriction should be considered, depending on the oil shock. Open to tightening but no call for an immediate hike; +1 rather than +2.

speaker: Ray Dalio
occasion: Bloomberg Television interview
quote: If there’s not a high enough real return, those bonds are not appreciated.
summary: Dalio said US debt is past the point of no return, that the bond market already shows early signs of a debt crisis (long rates rising versus short rates, weaker dollar, flows into gold), and that the resulting stagflation leaves the Fed in a very difficult position with Chair Warsh facing a test from the bond market. He said the path is heading toward 1930s-style financial repression. He also said equity bubble gauges are close to 1929 and 2000 levels and that all great technology changes produce bubbles.
old_note: Two-sided: investors need a higher real return now, but he expects eventual yield suppression by the central bank. No direct statement on the next rate move, so scored at 0.

speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
occasion: Fireside chat at a Kansas City Fed economic forum in Oklahoma
quote: The big question now is do we stay patient?
summary: Reuters (published June 5, quoting remarks made Thursday June 4) reports Schmid said inflation has probably crept up into the 3.50% range and asked aloud whether the Fed should stay patient or act by raising rates a quarter point or two to 'tamp this thing down'. FXStreet's same-day report calls inflation his biggest risk.
old_note: Openly weighing rate increases with inflation as the main risk, but framed as a question, not a call to hike.

speaker: David Mericle
occasion: Goldman Sachs Research report summarised on goldmansachs.com: 'Why the Fed Is Unlikely to Cut Rates This Year'
quote: A stronger starting point for the economy reduces the risk that a hike could end up looking like a costly mistake
summary: Goldman pushed its final two cuts to June and December 2027 (from December 2026 and March 2027), leaving the terminal rate at 3-3.25%. Mericle said unemployment rising only to 4.4% is not enough to create urgency to cut, and that hikes are unlikely but somewhat more likely than before.
old_note: Base case is a hold through 2026 with the next move a cut a year out; cuts were delayed and the bar for a hike was lowered. Torn between 0 and -1, chose 0.

speaker: Rick Rieder
occasion: Written commentary after the June FOMC, quoted by Morningstar
quote: While we don’t believe that a Fed hike is a given from here, we need to be respectful of that policy potential,
summary: Rieder took a more cautious view of the rate outlook than those reading the June dot plot as a hike signal. He expected a Warsh Fed with less forward guidance, less frequent communication and possibly no dot plot over time.
old_note: Hike not a given but possible; no directional call.

speaker: Tiffany Wilding
occasion: PIMCO Macro Signposts, 'Hawkish-Leaning Committee, Reform-Minded Chair: Warsh’s First Fed Meeting'
quote: If the agreement holds and lower oil prices prove durable, inflationary pressures – and the perceived case for hikes – should ease.
summary: PIMCO noted that nine of 18 dots showed a 2026 hike but even hawkish participants had not argued for an immediate hike, while 3-3.5% core PCE is inconsistent with cuts. It expects the Warsh Fed to bring fewer press conferences, less prescriptive communication and more rate volatility.
old_note: Neither hikes nor cuts expected near term; conditional easing of the hike case.

occasion: Client note on Monday 22 June, reported by Reuters (carried by The Standard HK)
quote: the Fed's reaction function is much more hawkish than we thought
summary: BofA switched from no change to 75bp of hikes in 2026 after the June projections and Warsh's comments, then a hold in 2027, saying inflation is likely to remain sticky. Per Fortune's account of the same note, the hikes are in September, October and December, to 4.25-4.5%.
old_note: Three hikes forecast.

occasion: Deutsche Bank research commentary quoted by FXStreet, 'Fed: Warsh signals tighter path'
quote: The central scenario sees two rate increases this year, likely in September and December, taking the fed funds rate to around 4.1%, followed by a prolonged pause through 2027.
summary: After the hawkish June FOMC and the shift in style under Warsh, Deutsche Bank's economists put two 25bp hikes into their forecast. The note observed that 9 of 18 dots signalled a 2026 hike and that 39bp of hikes were priced by December.
old_note: Two hikes forecast.

speaker: Rick Rieder
occasion: BlackRock Market Outlook, 'Getting Serious in Summer Markets'
quote: Another rate hike does not extract more oil or build more homes.
summary: Rieder argued the funds rate is powerful but uneven: it pressures borrowers, housing and lower-income consumers while the companies behind the AI capex cycle are far less rate-sensitive, and the categories driving inflation are largely rate-insensitive. He also called the new Fed's hawkish stance very understandable given above-target inflation.
old_note: Sceptical that hikes help (-1) but calls the hawkish stance understandable; torn, chose 0.

speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
occasion: Kansas City Fed Economic Forum, Grand Island, Nebraska: "The Federal Reserve, Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy"
quote: My primary concern is inflation, which is too hot and has been above target for too long.
summary: Schmid said the labor market is in balance and growth is resilient, so his focus in setting policy is inflation. He argued against the textbook habit of looking through supply-shock inflation (beef, energy) and against leaning on core measures.
old_note: Inflation is the primary concern and he rejects looking through supply shocks, but the text does not call for a rate increase outright, so +1 not +2.

speaker: Michael Gapen
occasion: Morgan Stanley Research article 'Watch Out for a Fed Pause' on morganstanley.com
quote: We expect a lower inflation trajectory that keeps policy on hold this year, potentially followed by two rate cuts in 2027 as inflation gradually normalizes
summary: Morgan Stanley Research expected the Fed to stay on hold in 2026 even though markets priced at least one hike, citing moderating inflation, a cooling labor market and market rates that had already tightened conditions. Gapen expected no hike in July and potentially two cuts in 2027.
old_note: Explicitly argues against the hike priced by markets and sees cuts as the next move.

speaker: Jamie Dimon
occasion: Master Investor Podcast with Wilfred Frost (recorded July 16, released July 20)

He put the appropriate short rate at 3.25-3.5% even with inflation at 2%, adding that rates are almost there today, and warned that debt and deficits will show up as higher interest rates and a rattled market.
old_note: He gives a level for where the short rate should be at 2% inflation and says policy is only about there while he distrusts the disinflation data, which implies policy is not restrictive. No explicit call for a hike, so +1 not +2. Date is the release date per Quartz (recorded July 16).

speaker: Michael Gapen
occasion: Thoughts on the Market podcast with Matthew Hornbach, 'Fed in July: A Weaker Case for Hiking' (transcript)

summary: Gapen expected the FOMC to keep the range at 3.5-3.75% in July because employment growth moderated and disinflation evidence appeared since June. If disinflation continues the Fed stays on hold; if inflation stays firm it can move to hikes later this year.
old_note: Forecast of a hold with two-sided conditionality.

speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
occasion: CNBC 'Closing Bell' interview after the July FOMC hold
quote: If you really want to get to 2%, I think you have to raise interest rates
summary: After the Fed held at 3.50-3.75% with three dissents for a hike, Gundlach said reaching 2% inflation requires raising rates and may not happen for a couple of years. He read the long-bond selloff during the press conference as bond vigilantes telling the Fed to back its rhetoric with action.
old_note: Says rates have to go up to reach the inflation target. CNBC's July 30 follow-up from the same interview carries his comment that corporate credit is softening with AI and tech spreads moving wider.

speaker: Michael Feroli
occasion: JPMorgan weekly prospects note sent to clients late Friday 31 July, reported by MarketWatch

summary: JPMorgan brought its next-hike call forward from the second half of 2027 to December 2026 after the July press conference, which it called the most troubling since press conferences began. Feroli expects the rest of the FOMC to feel it must defend the price stability mandate.
old_note: Brings a hike forward to December (not the next meeting) and flags September risk.

speaker: Alberto Musalem

The St. Louis Fed lists the FT interview as July 31; the Reuters copy opened is time-stamped Aug 1 India time.

summary: BofA economists wrote that the post-meeting price action (steeper curve, lower equities, weaker dollar) resembled a credibility shock of the kind emerging-market central banks face, and that the Fed has a growing credibility problem.

On private credit he walked through a fund markdown from 100 to 81, said some holdings must be worth close to zero, and described AI bond deals plus passive inflows as a dumping ground for overvalued IPOs.
old_note: The page is the firm's summary and only carries this short fragment in Gundlach's own words; the hike forecast itself is DoubleLine's paraphrase. Page timestamp is 01:42 UTC Aug 4 (Aug 3 ET).

speaker: Jeffrey Schmid

He also said the Fed should respond to aggregate inflation even when it comes from relative price rises tied to AI infrastructure demand.
old_note: Says policy is not restrictive and that tighter policy will be required: an explicit call for rate increases (made before the September hike).

speaker: Jamie Dimon

summary: Asked whether the long-end selloff is a credibility test for the Fed, Dimon said the real question is whether there is inflation, noted it has been over 3% for five years, and said the Fed will have to fight it if it persists. He backed Chair Warsh's review of inflation measurement and the balance sheet and dismissed complaints about the end of forward guidance. On credit he said market leverage (margin, prime broker, hedge fund) is high but not systemic, he is not worried about private credit systemically, and hyperscaler data-center spending will 'ultimately play out and pay out' though individual data-center projects need deal-by-deal analysis.
old_note: Conditional statement that the Fed will have to fight inflation, paired with his view that the odds favor higher inflation and rates. Leans tighter but no call for an immediate hike.

speaker: Susan Collins

She sees upside inflation risks from supply shocks and stronger activity, noting the AI build-out is lifting core goods prices.

quote: Hawkish rhetoric and patient policy can coexist, and we think they should.
summary: With the funds rate at 3.75-4.00%, Rieder said the remaining inflation hot spots (energy, insurance, healthcare, education, shelter) are areas where another 25bp hike is unlikely to have much effect, and that tightening further may cool rate-sensitive areas that are already cool. He noted AI-related debt is set to exceed the entire US high-yield market by end-2027.
old_note: Says the Fed should be patient rather than hike further.

speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
occasion: TomorrowX Summit, Austin (2026-11-17) · Iliana Bouzali
quote: The Fed is not cutting. They're hiking. We've had regime change at the Fed.
summary: Almost none of the January portfolio remains. In January fed funds were 3.5% against 6% nominal growth, so policy was ridiculously loose; now the Fed is hiking under Warsh, who is unhappy about 15 years of free money and five years of above-target inflation. 'So we have monetary tightening going on.'
old_note: 긴축이 진행 중이라는 현상 진단. 특정 회의 전망은 없어 7.5.

speaker: Michael Feroli
occasion: Client note on Thursday 19 November, reported by Reuters (carried by The Standard HK)
quote: These hikes aren't to deliver a bad labor market, but to preserve credibility when they have no compelling narrative for a pause,
summary: JPMorgan added quarter-point hikes in January and March 2027 to its December hike. It said Warsh has left the policy path without an overarching narrative, so policy is more likely to be reactive to data; the labor market has not been a source of inflation pressure yet inflation remains elevated.
old_note: Three consecutive hikes forecast.

speaker: Bill Ackman
role: Founder and CEO, Pershing Square Capital Management
occasion: Post on X ahead of the December FOMC
quote: The Fed will put the U.S. and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%
summary: Ackman said the Fed is about to make another mistake on December 9 if it hikes into sharply tighter financial conditions, noting a higher cost of equity and that SpaceX recently paid over 8% on secured debt. He called the 2% target misguided and 3% more realistic given military spending, de-globalization, tariffs and the AI infrastructure and energy buildout.
old_note: Opposes a December hike and further tightening. 'Another mistake' implies the September hike was one, which would fit -2, but he does not ask for cuts, so the level nearer 0 is used. X post not opened; the page gives no post date, so the article date is used.
